newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa wants more industry input on competition.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa wants more industry input on competition.

text.p: The South African government wants greater help from the private sector in its drive to make industry more competitive after years of inward-looking, import substitution strategies under apartheid rule.

The Department of Trade and Industry reported on Friday that after about 18 months of intensive research by 16 teams of researchers into specific industry clusters, it had evaluated their initial reports.
The reports were presented to Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin on Wednesday and he said he was satisfied with the progress that had been made.
"We are still learning and could not have expected to achieve more at this stage," he said in a statement.
The cluster studies are aimed at looking at the strengths and weaknesses of various industrial sectors and identifying ways in which they could become more competitive, with or without state help.

The statement said that some of the problems that had been encountered in the process included the lack of involvement by senior business leaders and the lack of a strategic agenda and marketing focus as well as customer segmentation.

It had now been decided to strengthen the research teams by appointing several new directors and detailed action plans were being drawn up for each cluster. These would be discussed with business leaders over the next two months.
"Our future actions and processes will be determined to a large extent on the response from industry," the department's chief director of industrial promotion Tony Hehr said.
He recently told a parliamentary committee that the cluster studies had had mixed results and needed to be refocused over the next year.

The government's emphasis on increasing the competitiveness of industry has been spurred on by repeated findings by the World Competitiveness Yearbook that South African industry was slipping down the competitiveness scale.
The finance sector, for example, had dropped from 23rd place out of a total of 46 countries in 1993 to 33rd place in 1996. Management had dropped to 43rd position from 32 in 1993.
"This does not mean that finance and management standards have dropped, but that the rest of the world has improved at a faster rate than South Africa," Hehr said.
"Given our past deficits, we have to run even harder to get ahead."

Possibly one of the most successful cluster studies has been that for the petrochemicals, plastics and synthetic fibers industries, but even members of that group have admitted that it had taken some time for business, labour and government to get used to talking to each other about their industries and ways in which they could be restructured to become more competitive.
But their discussions have already resulted in government introducing new tax incentives for new investments as well as special training programmes.
The cluster studies are largely being funded by a Japanese grant through the World Bank.
